overview.title: Learn
overview.intro: When you can’t place a digit, look for a candidate you can cross out. A few removals can leave a cell with only one choice.
difficultyParagraphs: Beginner, Easy, Medium, Tricky, Hard, Very Hard, Expert, Master, Extreme, and Impossible form our learning path. Medium is the starting difficulty for new players. Each level includes the techniques from earlier levels.
A difficulty describes the techniques used to solve a puzzle. Repeating an easy technique does not raise its level. Every level has one puzzle quality standard, with no separate workload setting.

Beginner focuses on visual scanning. Easy adds all singles. Medium introduces local candidate removals. Tricky follows one digit across houses, and Hard introduces wings. Very Hard starts chains and coloring; Expert and Master build general and grouped chains. Extreme combines forcing proofs and specialist patterns.
Impossible is our highest level. A skilled person may still solve these puzzles, but a practical human solution is not promised. Some may need extensive case analysis or computer help.
Foundation lessons come before the techniques that use them. Use Learn first on a technique page to find the concepts you need.

fundamentals.title: Fundamentals
fundamentals.summary: Read a cell address and work out which digits can go there.

paragraphs: Pick an empty cell with several placed digits in its row, column, or box. Cross off every digit those three houses already contain.
If one digit remains, you can place it. If several remain, try a cell whose houses contain more distinct digits.
A house is a row, a column, or a 3×3 box. Thick lines mark the boxes. Each house must contain the digits 1 through 9 once each. The digits you start with are called givens, or clues.
Every cell belongs to three houses. A line is either a row or a column.
Count rows down from the top and columns across from the left. Both counts start at 1. To find R2C4, go to row 2 and across to column 4.
Number the boxes across the top first, then across the middle, then across the bottom. The top-left box is box 1 and the bottom-right box is box 9.
Two cells that share a house see each other. They can’t hold the same digit. These cells are also called peers.
R2C4 shares row 2 with R2C5 and column 4 with R3C4. It also sees R3C5 through box 2.
The small digits in an empty cell are its candidates. To work them out, start with 1 through 9 and cross off the digits you find in the cell’s three houses.
The same markings appear in our lessons and hints. Learn their shapes and labels before you use the colors to follow a proof.

copy.description: Check R2C4. Row 2 rules out 2, 4, and 9.
copy.reason: Column 4 rules out five more digits, 1, 5, 6, 7, and 8. You’ve already crossed off the digits you see in box 2. Only 3 is left.

paragraphs: Place the 3. A cell with just one candidate gives you a naked single. This can also happen later, after another move lets you cross out a candidate.

blocks.title: Place a single
blocks.instruction: Pick an empty cell with one candidate. Enter that digit.

lessons.title: Which cells see each other?
lessons.summary: Trace a row, column, or box to find where a digit cannot go.

paragraphs: Pick a placed digit. Find the row, column, and box that contain it.
Two different cells that share a house are peers. Sudoku players say that the cells see each other.
If one cell contains 5, none of its peers can contain 5. Each shared house allows only one copy of the digit.

blocks.title: The same rule works before you place a digit

paragraphs: Suppose two peers both have a small candidate 5. If one candidate is correct, the other must go.
If you rule out one 5, its peer can still have other choices. A later lesson uses this conflict to build a weak link.

questions.prompt: R2C2 and R3C3 are on different rows and columns. Do they see each other?
questions.explanation: They share box 1. A single shared house is enough.

questions.prompt: R2C2 is 5. Does that placement rule out 5 from R4C4?
questions.explanation: The two cells share none of the three houses.

lessons.title: Full House
lessons.summary: Fill the last empty cell in a house.

paragraphs: Scan rows, columns, and boxes for a house with eight filled cells. Count which digit from 1 to 9 is missing.
If the house has two or more gaps, try a different house.
Look for a house with eight digits filled in. Check which digit from 1 to 9 is missing and put it in the gap.
For a box, count the nine cells inside its thick border. If you find two gaps in a house, check the candidates in each empty cell to see if one has a single choice.

lessons.title: Hidden Single in a Box
lessons.summary: Scan one box for the only place a digit can go.

paragraphs: Choose a digit that is missing from a box. Look at the rows and columns crossing its empty cells. If a row or column already contains that digit, it rules out those cells. When only one cell remains, place the digit there.

items: Start with a digit that already appears several times on the board.
Choose a box where it is missing.
Use matching digits outside the box to rule out rows and columns inside it.
Place the digit only when exactly one cell in the box can contain it.

paragraphs: Beginner puzzles combine this scanning technique with Full House. Easy adds Hidden Singles in rows and columns and Naked Singles, where you work through the candidates of one cell.

groups.title: Easy
groups.overview: Use all singles, including candidates in a cell and missing digits in lines.

lessons.title: Hidden Single
lessons.summary: Place a digit when it has only one possible cell in a house.

paragraphs: Pick a digit that already appears in several boxes. Find a box that still needs it and use the placed copies to rule out rows and columns.
If exactly one empty cell in the box can take the digit, place it there. You can also search one row or column at a time.
Choose a digit a house still needs. Check every empty cell in that house for it. If just one cell can take the digit, put it there. Other candidates in that cell make the single easy to miss.

items: In a row, look for copies of your digit in the crossing columns and boxes.
In a column, check the crossing rows and boxes.
In a box, follow the rows and columns through the box. A placed copy on either line rules out the cells it crosses.

lessons.title: Naked Single
lessons.summary: Place a digit when it’s the only candidate left in its cell.

paragraphs: Start with an empty cell that shares houses with many placed digits. Compare the digits already in its row, column, and box.
If those houses rule out eight different digits, place the one that remains. With candidates shown, look for a cell with one candidate.
Pick an empty cell. Cross off the digits you see in its three houses. One candidate left means you can fill the cell.
Check a cell again after you erase candidates. A pair, for instance, can cut a cell’s two candidates down to one.

lessons.title: Odd and even cells
lessons.summary: Remove candidates of the wrong parity from a marked cell.

paragraphs: Find a cell marked odd or even. Check the puzzle’s rule if you need to identify the mark.
Compare the candidates with the allowed digits. Odd cells can take 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9. Even cells can take 2, 4, 6, or 8.

copy.description: Read the parity clue under the grid. Compare it with the marked cell’s candidates.
copy.reason: A digit of the other parity cannot satisfy the clue. Remove it even if the ordinary row, column, and box still allow it.

guide.start: Find a cell marked odd or even. Check the puzzle’s rule if you need to identify the mark.
guide.check: Compare the candidates with the allowed digits. Odd cells can take 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9. Even cells can take 2, 4, 6, or 8.
guide.reason: A digit of the other parity cannot satisfy the clue. Remove it even if the ordinary row, column, and box still allow it.

lessons.title: Anti-King
lessons.summary: Use a chess king’s move to rule out repeated digits across touching corners.

paragraphs: Start at a placed digit near a box corner. Check the cells one row and one column away.
Look for the same digit as a candidate in those cells. The ordinary houses often cover the other king moves.

copy.description: Find the placed digit beside the highlighted cell on a diagonal.
copy.reason: The two cells are one king’s move apart, so they must differ. The placed digit rules out its matching candidate.

guide.start: Start at a placed digit near a box corner. Check the cells one row and one column away.
guide.check: Look for the same digit as a candidate in those cells. The ordinary houses often cover the other king moves.
guide.reason: The two cells are one king’s move apart, so they must differ. The placed digit rules out its matching candidate.

lessons.title: Anti-Knight
lessons.summary: Rule out repeated digits in cells a chess knight’s move apart.

paragraphs: Pick a placed digit. Move two cells up, down, left, or right, then one cell across at a right angle.
Check whether any reachable cell still shows that digit. Try the same move from other placed digits.

copy.description: Use a two-by-one move to find which placed digit rules out the crossed-out candidate.
copy.reason: A pair of cells a knight’s move apart must contain different digits. Remove the placed digit from the candidates in the other cell.

guide.start: Pick a placed digit. Move two cells up, down, left, or right, then one cell across at a right angle.
guide.check: Check whether any reachable cell still shows that digit. Try the same move from other placed digits.
guide.reason: A pair of cells a knight’s move apart must contain different digits. Remove the placed digit from the candidates in the other cell.

lessons.title: Non-consecutive neighbors
lessons.summary: Keep digits that differ by one out of cells that share an edge.

paragraphs: Start with a placed digit. Check its neighbors above, below, left, and right.
Look for candidates one less or one more than that digit. For 1, check only 2. For 9, check only 8.

copy.description: Compare the highlighted neighbors through their shared edge.
copy.reason: A shared edge rules out candidates that differ from the placed digit by one. The row or column already rules out a repeat.

guide.start: Start with a placed digit. Check its neighbors above, below, left, and right.
guide.check: Look for candidates one less or one more than that digit. For 1, check only 2. For 9, check only 8.
guide.reason: A shared edge rules out candidates that differ from the placed digit by one. The row or column already rules out a repeat.

lessons.title: Inequality
lessons.summary: Use a less-than clue to compare the candidate lists in two cells.

paragraphs: Read the two cells in the clue. The cell before the less-than sign needs the smaller digit.
Compare each candidate in the smaller cell with the largest option in the larger cell. Then compare each larger candidate with the smallest option.

copy.description: Use the less-than clue below the board to check the two highlighted cells.
copy.reason: A candidate fails if no value in the other cell can satisfy the inequality with it. Keep the candidates that have at least one partner.

guide.start: Read the two cells in the clue. The cell before the less-than sign needs the smaller digit.
guide.check: Compare each candidate in the smaller cell with the largest option in the larger cell. Then compare each larger candidate with the smallest option.
guide.reason: A candidate fails if no value in the other cell can satisfy the inequality with it. Keep the candidates that have at least one partner.

lessons.title: Clone cells
lessons.summary: Keep only the digits that every cell in a clone group can share.

paragraphs: Find a group of cells marked to have the same digit. Compare the candidates at matching positions.
If one cell has a placed digit, check that digit in all its copies. Otherwise, find the digits common to every candidate list.

copy.description: The clue under the board lists the cells that must take the same digit.
copy.reason: All cells in the group must take the same value. A digit missing from any one cell cannot go in the others.

guide.start: Find a group of cells marked to have the same digit. Compare the candidates at matching positions.
guide.check: If one cell has a placed digit, check that digit in all its copies. Otherwise, find the digits common to every candidate list.
guide.reason: All cells in the group must take the same value. A digit missing from any one cell cannot go in the others.

lessons.title: Kropki dots
lessons.summary: Check which candidate pairs fit a white or black dot.

paragraphs: Pick a marked pair with few candidates. Read a white dot as a difference of one and a black dot as a ratio of two to one.
Try each candidate with the options across the dot. If the pair has both dots, it must use 1 and 2.

copy.description: Read the dot between the marked cells. Keep only candidates that belong to a pair that fits the dot.
copy.reason: Any candidate without a matching partner violates the dot. Cross it out and check whether this leaves the other cell with fewer choices.

guide.start: Pick a marked pair with few candidates. Read a white dot as a difference of one and a black dot as a ratio of two to one.
guide.check: Try each candidate with the options across the dot. If the pair has both dots, it must use 1 and 2.
guide.reason: Any candidate without a matching partner violates the dot. Cross it out and check whether this leaves the other cell with fewer choices.

lessons.title: XV sums
lessons.summary: Keep the candidate pairs that sum to 5 at a V or 10 at an X.

paragraphs: Find an X or V between two cells. Start with the pair that has a placed digit or the shorter candidate lists.
Subtract each candidate in the first cell from the marked sum. Check whether the result fits in the second cell.

copy.description: Read the X or V clue and its two cell addresses under the grid.
copy.reason: If the other cell has no candidate that completes the total, the first candidate cannot satisfy the clue.

guide.start: Find an X or V between two cells. Start with the pair that has a placed digit or the shorter candidate lists.
guide.check: Subtract each candidate in the first cell from the marked sum. Check whether the result fits in the second cell.
guide.reason: If the other cell has no candidate that completes the total, the first candidate cannot satisfy the clue.

lessons.title: Palindrome lines
lessons.summary: Match candidates in cells the same distance from opposite ends of a line.

paragraphs: Start at the first and last cells of the line. Those cells must contain the same digit.
Move one step inward from each end and repeat. Keep only the digits that both cells of each pair can take.

copy.description: Use the ordered cell list below the board. Compare positions from opposite ends of that list.
copy.reason: The line must read the same in both directions. A candidate whose mirror cannot take the same digit can go.

guide.start: Start at the first and last cells of the line. Those cells must contain the same digit.
guide.check: Move one step inward from each end and repeat. Keep only the digits that both cells of each pair can take.
guide.reason: The line must read the same in both directions. A candidate whose mirror cannot take the same digit can go.

lessons.title: Between lines
lessons.summary: Use the endpoints to bound every digit inside the line.

paragraphs: Find the two endpoints and compare their candidates. The line can run from the smaller endpoint to the larger one in either direction.
For each possible endpoint pair, check which candidates lie strictly between the two values. Every interior cell needs an option within that range.

copy.description: The first and last cells in the clue are the endpoints. Compare them with the highlighted interior.
copy.reason: A candidate can go if no allowed endpoint pair leaves it between the endpoints. An endpoint value can also go if every pairing that uses it fails.

guide.start: Find the two endpoints and compare their candidates. The line can run from the smaller endpoint to the larger one in either direction.
guide.check: For each possible endpoint pair, check which candidates lie strictly between the two values. Every interior cell needs an option within that range.
guide.reason: A candidate can go if no allowed endpoint pair leaves it between the endpoints. An endpoint value can also go if every pairing that uses it fails.

lessons.title: Thermometers
lessons.summary: Use strictly increasing digits from the bulb to the tip.

paragraphs: Count the cells on a thermometer. Start at the bulb, where the smallest digit on the line must go.
Allow room for a higher digit at every step. Work backwards from the tip to limit the earlier cells.

copy.description: Read the thermometer from the round bulb to the tip. Check how many increasing steps a crossed-out candidate leaves room for.
copy.reason: A candidate must have a smaller choice before it and a larger choice after it where those neighbors exist. Remove candidates that cannot fit an increasing sequence.

guide.start: Count the cells on a thermometer. Start at the bulb, where the smallest digit on the line must go.
guide.check: Allow room for a higher digit at every step. Work backwards from the tip to limit the earlier cells.
guide.reason: A candidate must have a smaller choice before it and a larger choice after it where those neighbors exist. Remove candidates that cannot fit an increasing sequence.

lessons.title: Killer cage combinations
lessons.summary: Keep assignments that reach a cage total with distinct digits.

paragraphs: Pick a small dashed cage with an unusual total. List sets of distinct digits of the right size that add to that total.
Try to fit each set to the individual cells. Remove a set if some digit in it has no valid slot or several digits need the same slot.

copy.description: Read the small total in the cage corner. Check the highlighted cells against complete cage assignments.
copy.reason: A candidate needs a full assignment that uses it in its own cell. A digit can fit the cage total and still have no way to fit that cell.

guide.start: Pick a small dashed cage with an unusual total. List sets of distinct digits of the right size that add to that total.
guide.check: Try to fit each set to the individual cells. Remove a set if some digit in it has no valid slot or several digits need the same slot.
guide.reason: A candidate needs a full assignment that uses it in its own cell. A digit can fit the cage total and still have no way to fit that cell.

lessons.title: Arrows
lessons.summary: Match the sum of the arrow’s path to the digit in its circle.

paragraphs: Start with the circle’s candidates and count the cells on the arrow. A long arrow needs a total large enough to fit all its cells.
Try combinations along the arrow and compare their sums with the circle. Apply the usual house rules to any cells that see each other.

copy.description: The circle gives the total. Follow the arrow and check which path digits can add to that total.
copy.reason: A candidate belongs only if it fits a full assignment with that sum. You can remove candidates from the circle and the path.

guide.start: Start with the circle’s candidates and count the cells on the arrow. A long arrow needs a total large enough to fit all its cells.
guide.check: Try combinations along the arrow and compare their sums with the circle. Apply the usual house rules to any cells that see each other.
guide.reason: A candidate belongs only if it fits a full assignment with that sum. You can remove candidates from the circle and the path.

groups.title: Medium
groups.overview: Remove candidates using intersections and small sets.

lessons.title: Candidates and eliminations
lessons.summary: Use complete notes to prove what a cell cannot contain.

paragraphs: Start after singles stop. Check that your notes include every digit still possible in each cell you will use.
A missing pencil mark is not proof that a digit is impossible. Partial notes can create a false pair or a false strong link.
A candidate is a digit that remains possible. An elimination proves that one specific digit cannot occupy one specific cell.
After an elimination, check both the cell and its houses for singles. A useful elimination does not have to place a digit immediately.

blocks.caption: One cell, two different claims
rows: A proof rules out that particular 8.
Every valid completion must put 8 there.

paragraphs: Suppose two cells in row 3 each contain only {2, 8}. They need both digits, although their order is unknown.
Together they reserve 2 and 8 for those cells. Later subset lessons extend this counting argument to more cells.
Count distinct digits across the cells. Two copies of candidate 2 still count as one digit.

questions.prompt: A cell has notes {2, 8}, but you never checked whether 5 fits. Is this a proven two-choice cell?
questions.explanation: The notes are incomplete. Check 5 before using a two-choice argument.

questions.prompt: An elimination creates no single. Can it still be useful?
questions.explanation: It reduces the remaining possibilities and can make another pattern available.

questions.prompt: Two cells contain {2, 8} and {2, 8}. How many distinct candidate digits are there?
questions.explanation: The distinct digits are 2 and 8. Repeated pencil marks do not add new digits.

lessons.title: Locked Candidates
lessons.summary: Erase a candidate when its only places in one house are also in another.

paragraphs: Highlight one digit and look for a box where all its candidates line up in one row or column. This is the start of pointing.
For claiming, start with a row or column whose candidates for that digit all fall in one box. Continue if the other house still has the digit as a candidate outside the overlap.
A line crosses three cells of a box. When one house has to put a digit in those three cells, both houses get the digit from that placement.

Check where a digit can go in the box. If all its candidates sit on one line, erase the digit from that line outside the box. Two candidates in the box make a pointing pair. Three make a pointing triple.
Read along a row or column. If all its candidates for your digit sit inside one box, the line has claimed that box’s copy. Erase the digit from the rest of the box.

lessons.title: Counting cells and digits
lessons.summary: Use an equal count to find cells or digits that are reserved for each other.

paragraphs: Choose a house with several short candidate lists. Pick two or three cells in that house. Count the different digits across their lists.
Each selected cell needs a digit. A house can use each digit only once.
If three cells have only three different digits between them, those cells need all three digits. The order can still vary.
Suppose row 6 needs 3 and 8. Only R6C2 and R6C6 can contain either digit.
Both digits must fit in those two cells. You can remove every other digit from those cells.

blocks.caption: Two ways to count
rows: As many distinct digits as cells
Those digits in other cells of the house
Selected missing digits in a house
As many possible cells as digits

questions.prompt: Three cells in a row have {2, 4}, {4, 7}, and {2, 7}. How many distinct digits do they have?
questions.explanation: The digits are 2, 4, and 7. Count each digit once.

questions.prompt: In one box, 2 and 9 can only go in the same two cells. Where can you remove other digits?
options: From the rest of the box
questions.explanation: Those two cells must contain 2 and 9 in some order.

questions.prompt: Three selected cells have four distinct candidates. Does that count reserve all four digits for them?
questions.explanation: Three cells can use only three digits. The count alone cannot tell you which digit is absent.

lessons.title: Naked Subsets
lessons.summary: When several cells have just enough digits to fill them, erase those digits from the rest of the house.

paragraphs: Pick a house with several short candidate lists. Start with two cells that each have the same two candidates.
For a triple or quadruple, add cells whose candidates mostly repeat digits you have already counted. Continue when the number of distinct digits matches the number of cells.
If the cells all sit in the overlap of a line and a box, look for removals in both houses.
Pick cells in one house and count the different digits in their candidate lists. Three cells with only three digits between them have to use all three. The same count works with two or four cells.
Two cells each show only 4 and 6. Whichever takes 4, the other takes 6. Erase 4 and 6 from the rest of the house.
A triple could have cells with 2 and 3, 2 and 5, and 3 and 5. Together they need all of 2, 3, and 5. Erase those digits from the rest of the house.
The lists 12, 24, 34, and 123 contain only four distinct digits. In one house, those four cells take up 1, 2, 3, and 4. Erase the four digits elsewhere in the house.
When both cells sit where a line crosses a box, the pair uses its digits in both houses. Erase them from the other cells of the line and the box.
Three cells can also fill the stretch where a line crosses a box. Erase the triple’s digits in both houses. A quadruple is too large for that three-cell overlap.

lessons.title: Hidden Subsets
lessons.summary: If several digits have only the same few cells available, erase the other candidates from those cells.

paragraphs: In one house, pick a missing digit with only two or three possible cells. Look for other missing digits whose candidates fit inside that same small set of cells.
Continue if the number of cells equals the number of chosen digits. Look inside those cells for candidates outside the chosen digits.
Start with digits a house still needs. Count every cell that can take at least one of your chosen digits. If there are as many cells as digits, those cells are all spoken for.
When two digits can only go in the same two cells, those cells have to take the pair. Check all nine cells of the house before you erase the other candidates in those two cells.
Count the cells that can take any of three digits. If there are exactly three such cells in the house, erase their other candidates. A cell can show any one, two, or all three of the chosen digits.
Try four digits that appear only a few times each. Before you erase the other candidates from their four cells, scan the whole house for another copy of any of the chosen digits.

lessons.title: Whispers lines
lessons.summary: Check the minimum difference required between neighbors on a line.

paragraphs: Read the minimum difference from the clue. German Whispers usually use 5. Start at a placed digit or a cell with few options.
For each candidate, find a neighbor’s candidate that differs by at least the required amount. Check both neighbors for an interior cell.

copy.description: Use the clue under the grid to follow the line and read its minimum difference.
copy.reason: A candidate needs a valid partner on every Whispers edge it touches. If one edge cannot reach the minimum difference, remove the candidate.

guide.start: Read the minimum difference from the clue. German Whispers usually use 5. Start at a placed digit or a cell with few options.
guide.check: For each candidate, find a neighbor’s candidate that differs by at least the required amount. Check both neighbors for an interior cell.
guide.reason: A candidate needs a valid partner on every Whispers edge it touches. If one edge cannot reach the minimum difference, remove the candidate.

lessons.title: Renban lines
lessons.summary: Fit the line’s cells into a set of consecutive digits in any order.

paragraphs: Count the cells on the line. For a three-cell Renban, try candidate sets such as 1, 2, 3 or 5, 6, 7.
Check whether each consecutive set can give each cell a different valid digit. Any given digit on the line must belong to the set.

copy.description: Use the ordered cells below the board to find the whole Renban. Check all valid consecutive ranges.
copy.reason: A candidate must belong to a consecutive set that fits all the line cells. The cells can appear in any order along the line.

guide.start: Count the cells on the line. For a three-cell Renban, try candidate sets such as 1, 2, 3 or 5, 6, 7.
guide.check: Check whether each consecutive set can give each cell a different valid digit. Any given digit on the line must belong to the set.
guide.reason: A candidate must belong to a consecutive set that fits all the line cells. The cells can appear in any order along the line.

lessons.title: Region Sum lines
lessons.summary: Match the total in every segment of a line across box boundaries.

paragraphs: Trace the line and split it at each region boundary. If the puzzle groups repeat visits by region, combine those visits.
Start with a short segment. List its possible totals and keep only totals that every segment can reach.

copy.description: Read the line’s cell list and group the cells by the boundaries it crosses.
copy.reason: A candidate is valid only if its segment can reach a shared total with it. A one-cell segment can fix the sum for the rest of the line.

guide.start: Trace the line and split it at each region boundary. If the puzzle groups repeat visits by region, combine those visits.
guide.check: Start with a short segment. List its possible totals and keep only totals that every segment can reach.
guide.reason: A candidate is valid only if its segment can reach a shared total with it. A one-cell segment can fix the sum for the rest of the line.

lessons.title: Killer cage and house sums
lessons.summary: Subtract cage totals from a house total of 45 to find the sum of shared or leftover cells.

paragraphs: Pick a row, column, or box that contains several full cages. Add their totals and compare the result with 45.
If cages cross the house boundary, count which cells are inside and outside. The sum of the outside cells is the cage total minus the inside total.

copy.description: Follow the highlighted boundary. Use the cage totals to find the sum that the highlighted cells must reach.
copy.reason: Every house contains the digits 1 through 9, so its total is 45. Subtract known totals to get a new sum, then check the remaining candidates against it.

guide.start: Pick a row, column, or box that contains several full cages. Add their totals and compare the result with 45.
guide.check: If cages cross the house boundary, count which cells are inside and outside. The sum of the outside cells is the cage total minus the inside total.
guide.reason: Every house contains the digits 1 through 9, so its total is 45. Subtract known totals to get a new sum, then check the remaining candidates against it.

lessons.title: Little Killer sums
lessons.summary: Use the sum clue for a diagonal ray.

paragraphs: Start with the clue’s cells in order. Add the placed digits and subtract them from the clue total.
Find the smallest and largest totals the empty cells can still reach. Check candidates against the remaining sum and the houses the ray crosses.

copy.description: The clue lists the diagonal cells in reading order. Only those cells contribute to the sum.
copy.reason: Every candidate on the ray needs a way to complete the total. Digits can repeat along the ray if their cells share no house.

guide.start: Start with the clue’s cells in order. Add the placed digits and subtract them from the clue total.
guide.check: Find the smallest and largest totals the empty cells can still reach. Check candidates against the remaining sum and the houses the ray crosses.
guide.reason: Every candidate on the ray needs a way to complete the total. Digits can repeat along the ray if their cells share no house.

groups.title: Tricky
groups.overview: Follow one digit across several houses.

lessons.title: Strong and weak links
lessons.summary: See why one candidate rules out another, and why the last remaining choice must be true.

paragraphs: Highlight one digit. Find a house where it has exactly two remaining places. Then find a house where it has three.
A candidate such as 5 at R4C2 is a statement about the solution. It is true if the solution has 5 there.
A link describes what one candidate tells you about another.
Our diagrams use solid lines for strong links and dashed lines for weak links. An arrow shows the direction of the reasoning.
Rings mark the candidates in the example. The captions tell you which states follow from a temporary assumption.

blocks.title: A weak link comes from a conflict

paragraphs: A row can contain only one copy of each digit. If R4C2 is 5, R4C5 cannot be 5. The same rule works in the other direction.
A cell can hold only one digit. If a cell is 2, it cannot also be 7.
These are weak links. A true end forces the other end false. Both ends can be false if a third choice remains.

blocks.title: A strong link comes from a required choice

paragraphs: Row 4 must contain a 5. If R4C2 and R4C8 are its only places, ruling out R4C2 forces 5 into R4C8.
This is a strong link. A false end forces the other end true. At least one end must be true.
Check the whole house for the digit. A third candidate in that house breaks this reason for a strong link.

blocks.title: One pair can have both links

paragraphs: The two places for 5 in row 4 also conflict. Exactly one must be true. A pair with both properties has a dual link.
The same rule applies in a cell with only two candidates. The cell needs a digit and can hold only one.

blocks.caption: Which truth combinations does each link allow?

paragraphs: A weak link proves a conflict. A strong link proves that at least one end is true.
Some later proofs give a strong link whose ends can both be true. Use it as a weak link only if the two ends also conflict.
In Skyscraper, two row pairs each need a 5. The two candidates in the shared column conflict. Those three links work together.
In wings and chains, links can also switch digits inside a cell. Follow the rule for the link you are using.

questions.prompt: Three cells in a row can contain 7. One loses 7. Must a particular other cell now be 7?
questions.explanation: Two places remain. The weak link does not force either one.

questions.prompt: A cell contains exactly {3, 9}. Which relationship joins its candidates?
questions.explanation: One must be true and they cannot both be true.

questions.prompt: A proof establishes a strong link but no conflict between its ends. Can both ends be true?
questions.explanation: A strong link only rules out both ends being false. A separate conflict is needed for a weak link.

references.label: Pure Sudoku: propositions and inference chains

lessons.title: Counting rows and columns
lessons.summary: See why equal numbers of rows and columns reserve every place for one digit.

paragraphs: Highlight one missing digit. Choose rows that have few places for that digit. Read all nine cells in each chosen row.

blocks.title: The rows need a place each

paragraphs: The selected rows are the bases. Each base needs one copy of the digit.
The columns that contain every candidate in those rows are the covers. Each cover can hold at most one copy.
If the number of bases and covers matches, the bases need every cover. This is the count behind a basic fish.

blocks.title: Where the count removes a candidate

paragraphs: A candidate outside the base rows cannot use one of the cover columns. The base rows need that column for the same digit.
You can start with columns as the bases instead. Then the rows are the covers.

questions.prompt: Three chosen rows need a 5 each. All their 5s fit in the same three columns. Must all three columns get a 5 from those rows?
questions.explanation: Each row needs one 5. The three placements must use different columns.

questions.prompt: One of those rows has another 5 in a fourth column. Does the same count still reserve the first three columns?
questions.explanation: The extra candidate gives the row a place outside those covers. The basic fish count needs all base candidates inside its covers.

lessons.title: X-Wing
lessons.summary: Look for two rows that use the same two columns for a digit, or the same pattern turned sideways.

paragraphs: Pick one digit. Find a row with exactly two places for it and scan the other rows for the same two columns.
A row with a few extra candidates in one box is worth checking for a fin. If a corner is missing, check the sashimi version. You can start with columns as well.
Look for a digit with exactly two places in each of two rows, lined up in the same columns. One row takes one column and the other takes the second. That uses up both columns for this digit.
With a pair of rows, erase the digit from both columns outside those rows. If you spot the rectangle by checking two columns first, erase from the crossing rows outside those columns.

The four corners can come with extra candidates, called fins, outside the crossing lines. All fins must share a box. A target sits in that box on a crossing line, outside the starting lines. If a fin takes the digit, the box rules out the target. If all fins are gone, the X-Wing rules it out.

Set the fins aside and look at what’s left of the rectangle. With a sashimi, one starting line has only one corner left. That corner fixes the digit in one crossing line, and the other starting line uses the second. Check for removals in the same part of the fin box.

lessons.title: Skyscraper
lessons.summary: Find two rows with two places each for a digit and one pair of ends in the same column.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and find two rows with exactly two places each for it. Look for pairs with one column in common and different columns at the other ends.
Continue if another candidate for the digit can see both of those other ends. You can turn the same search sideways.
Pick a digit with two candidates in each of two rows. Find a candidate in one row directly above the matching candidate in the other. The two far ends must sit in different columns.
The row pairs supply strong links. The aligned candidates in the shared column supply a weak link.
If one far end is false, its row forces the aligned candidate true. That rules out the other aligned candidate and forces the other far end.
At least one far end must be true. Remove the digit from any cell that sees both far ends. The same logic works with rows and columns swapped.

lessons.title: Two-String Kite
lessons.summary: Join a row pair and a column pair for one digit through the box they share.

paragraphs: Find a row with exactly two places for one digit. Look for a column with exactly two places for the same digit.
Continue if one end of each pair shares a box with the other. Check whether another candidate sees both far ends.

Find a row and a column with exactly two places each for the same digit. You need four different cells, with one end from each pair in the same box. Only one of those ends can take the digit, so at least one far end has to take it.

For each kite, erase the digit from cells that see both far ends. A second pair can use the same joining cells in the box. Trace the two kites separately so you use the right far ends for each removal.

lessons.title: Empty Rectangle
lessons.summary: Use a box’s two candidate lines and a pair outside it to erase a candidate.

paragraphs: Pick one digit in a box. Look for candidates that all fit on one row and one column, with candidates on both arms.
Look outside the box for a row or column with only two places for that digit. Continue if one end lines up with an arm of the box.

Pick one digit in a box. All its candidates must fit along one row and one column, with marks on both arms. The four cells off those lines give the pattern its name. The cell where the arms meet can also show the digit.

Find a line outside the box with only two places for the digit. One end of the pair must line up with one arm. If that end takes the digit, the box has to put its copy on the other arm. Look for a target on that other arm’s line that also sees the far end of the pair. Either placement rules it out.

You can start from either arm. If the target and the far end are the only two places for the digit in their line, follow the same argument backwards for a second removal. When the box has just two candidates, you can also read the pattern as a short X-Chain.

lessons.title: Swordfish
lessons.summary: Find a digit that three rows can place only in the same three columns.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and mark the columns it can use in rows with two or three places for it. Start with two rows whose candidates mostly line up.
Look for a third row that fits the same three columns. If some candidates fall outside those columns, keep looking only if those extras share one box. You can also start with columns.

Look across three rows for one digit. Each row must have at least two candidates, and together they can use only three columns. Those rows need three copies in distinct columns. Erase the other candidates in those columns. You can also start with three columns and erase from the crossing rows.

Set aside the candidates outside the crossing lines. If they all sit in one box and you can see an ordinary Swordfish without them, check where the crossing lines enter that box. Erase only outside the starting lines. A fin in the box rules out the target if it takes the digit, and the Swordfish rules it out if all fins are gone.

If at least one starting line has just one candidate once you set the fins aside, you have a sashimi. That candidate fixes one of the three placements. The others still have to use different crossing lines. Look for the same targets as in the finned version.

groups.title: Hard
groups.overview: Recognize wings and other fixed patterns.

lessons.title: Bivalue cells and cases
lessons.summary: Use every possible value of a cell to prove a result.

paragraphs: Find a cell with exactly two candidates, called a bivalue cell. Look for nearby bivalue cells that share one of its candidates.
Suppose a pivot has {2, 6}. A peer A has {2, 9}, and another peer B has {6, 9}.
If the pivot is 2, A must be 9. If the pivot is 6, B must be 9. These are all choices for the pivot.
At least one of A and B is 9. A target that sees both cannot be 9. You do not have to decide which case is correct.
These are hypothetical branches of one proof. Do not place the pivot value on the real board while you examine a branch.

blocks.title: Check the target in every case

paragraphs: Seeing only A is not enough: the other case forces B. If the pivot also contains 9, you need a third case.
This is the reasoning behind wings. Their shapes help you find this proof quickly.

questions.prompt: A pivot has {2, 6}. Both cases remove 9 from the same target. Can you remove that 9?
questions.explanation: All possible pivot values lead to the same removal.

questions.prompt: The pivot has {2, 6, 9}, but you checked only 2 and 6. Is the proof complete?
questions.explanation: The pivot can still be 9. That case needs its own argument.

questions.prompt: One case forces A=9 and the other forces B=9. A target sees A but not B. Is its 9 removed?
questions.explanation: The target must conflict with the forced result in every case.

lessons.title: XY-Wing
lessons.summary: Either digit in the pivot makes one of the wings take their common digit.

paragraphs: Pick a cell with two candidates. For each of those digits, look for a cell it sees with exactly two candidates, one of which is that digit.
Continue if the two outside cells share the same extra digit. Look for another cell with that digit that sees both outside cells.
In the example, the middle cell, or pivot, has 1 and 2. Look for two cells that see it. One has only 1 and 3 and the other has only 2 and 3. Those two cells are the wings.

A 1 in the pivot leaves the 1 and 3 wing with 3. A 2 leaves the other wing with 3. Erase 3 anywhere that sees both wings. Check each wing against the pivot separately. They can see it through different houses.

lessons.title: XYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: The pivot holds the wings’ common digit, so a target has to see all three cells.

paragraphs: Pick a cell with three candidates. Look for two cells it sees that each contain only two of those three digits.
Continue if the pairs share one digit and together cover all three. A target must have that shared digit and see all three cells.
The pivot in the figure has 2, 8, and 9. The wings see the pivot and have only 2 and 8, or 8 and 9. If the pivot takes 2 or 9, one wing takes 8. The pivot could also take 8 itself.
Erase 8 from a cell that sees all three. R6C5 sees the wing in R2C5 through column 5, and sees the pivot and the other wing through the middle box.

lessons.title: W-Wing
lessons.summary: Link two cells with the same two candidates so one wing must take the other digit.

paragraphs: Find two cells that have the same two candidates. Pick one of those digits and look for a house with exactly two places for it.
Keep looking if each end of that pair sees a different starting cell. A target for the other digit must see both starting cells.
In the figure, both wings have 5 and 7. Column 2 has just two places for 7, and each of those places sees a different wing. Whichever place takes 7 leaves the wing it sees with only 5.
Erase 5 in any cell that sees both wings. If you find a house with two places for 5 instead, use that link to look for a removal of 7.

lessons.title: Jellyfish
lessons.summary: Find a digit that four rows can place only in the same four columns.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and start with rows whose candidates fall in only a few columns. Add rows that reuse those columns.
Check for four rows that use four columns between them. For a finned version, all candidates outside those four columns must share a box. You can also start with columns.

Pick a digit and four rows with at least two candidates each. Count the distinct columns that contain those candidates. If the count is four, those four rows use up the columns for that digit. Erase the other copies in the columns. Four starting columns work the same way.

If you have a Jellyfish plus a few extra candidates outside the crossing lines, check where the extras are. They must all be in one box. The target is in that box and on a crossing line, outside the starting lines. It loses if a fin takes the digit and if the Jellyfish uses up the crossing lines.

When you set the fins aside, one or more starting lines can be left with just one candidate. Those candidates fix some of the placements. All four starting lines still need different crossing lines. Use the same target area as for a finned Jellyfish.

lessons.title: The uniqueness assumption
lessons.summary: Understand the extra promise behind uniqueness techniques.

paragraphs: Before using a uniqueness technique, make sure the puzzle has exactly one solution. Sudoku rules alone do not guarantee this.
Imagine four empty cells at R1C2, R1C3, R4C2, and R4C3, each restricted to {1, 7}. They occupy two rows, two columns, and two boxes.
If one valid completion fills them in an alternating pattern, swapping 1 and 7 in all four preserves each affected house.
The swap leaves all other cells unchanged. It would give a second valid completion, contradicting a known promise of uniqueness.
Unique Rectangle and BUG techniques use this extra promise. Ordinary singles, subsets, and link arguments do not need it.
A rectangle spanning four boxes does not support this swap argument. Givens cannot be swapped. Variant rules can also make the swap invalid.
For imported or unfinished custom puzzles, verify uniqueness before using these techniques. Finding one solution is not enough.

questions.prompt: A solver finds one completed grid and stops. Does that prove uniqueness?
questions.explanation: Another completion might still exist. Uniqueness requires ruling out a second solution.

questions.prompt: Can ordinary candidate conflicts be used without assuming a unique solution?
questions.explanation: They follow from the Sudoku rules and apply to every valid completion.

questions.prompt: A proposed swap changes a given digit. Is it a valid uniqueness argument?
questions.explanation: Every valid completion must preserve the givens.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle
lessons.summary: Look for four corners where swapping two digits would give a second solution.

paragraphs: On a puzzle with one solution, start at a cell with only two candidates. Look for that same pair in a second cell in its row or column.
Look across those lines for two more cells that both contain the pair. Continue if the four corners span exactly two boxes. The extra candidates and strong links tell you which version to use.

Use this on a puzzle with exactly one solution. Look for four empty corners in two rows and two columns, across exactly two boxes. All four can take the same two digits. If they used only those digits, each diagonal would hold one of them. You could swap the two digits without changing which digits any house contains. At least one corner has to use an extra digit to prevent that swap.

blocks.title: Type 1 with extras in one corner

paragraphs: If three corners have only the pair, the fourth has to use an extra digit. Erase both digits of the pair from that corner.

blocks.title: Type 2 with the same extra on adjacent corners

paragraphs: Look for two neighboring corners with the same extra digit and the other two corners with just the pair. One of the two extras must be placed. Erase that digit in any cell that sees both corners with the extra.

blocks.title: Type 3 with a subset of extra digits

paragraphs: Two adjacent corners have extras, and between them they need at least one extra digit. Count the two corners as one slot for those digits. Add cells from a house they share until the number of distinct digits equals the number of slots. Erase those digits from the other cells of that house.

blocks.title: Type 4 with a strong link on one side

paragraphs: Two adjacent corners have extras. Look for a digit of the rectangle pair that has only those two places in a shared house. One corner must take it. If the other corner took the second digit of the pair, all four corners would use only the pair. Erase the second digit from both corners with extras.

blocks.title: Type 5 with the same extra across the diagonals

paragraphs: Find the same extra digit in two opposite corners or in three corners, with no other extras. At least one of those corners must take the extra. Erase it from any cell that sees all the corners where it appears.

blocks.title: Type 6 with one digit locked to a diagonal

paragraphs: The two corners with extras are opposite each other. Find a digit of the pair whose only places in both rows and both columns are the four corners. It must take one whole diagonal. If it took the diagonal with extras, the other two corners would take the second digit and allow the swap. Erase the linked digit from the corners with extras.

Start at a corner that contains just the pair and look at the opposite corner. One digit of the pair must have no places beyond the rectangle in that opposite corner’s row and column. If the opposite corner took the other digit, both lines would force the rectangle into the swappable arrangement. Erase that other digit from the opposite corner.

The swap can also involve digits you’ve already placed. Check that none of the corners is a given. With three filled corners, erase the candidate that would complete the swap. With two filled corners and the same extra candidate in both empty corners, erase that extra from cells that see both empty corners.

The swap has to respect the givens. A rectangle digit might have been crossed out during an earlier move even though the givens allow it there. Check that both digits could go in all four corners from the givens before you use this version.

lessons.title: BUG+1
lessons.summary: In a puzzle with one solution, look for the extra candidate that keeps all the empty cells from having two choices.

paragraphs: Scan the empty cells for short candidate lists. Keep looking if exactly one cell has three candidates and every other empty cell has two.
In the row, column, and box of the three-candidate cell, count the possible spots for each of its digits. Look for the digit that has three spots in all three houses.

BUG stands for Bivalue Universal Grave. In a BUG, every empty cell has two candidates and every missing digit has two places in each house that needs it. If you solved that grid, changing every originally empty cell to its other digit would still leave one of each digit in every house. You’d have two solutions.

For BUG+1, look for one cell with three candidates and two candidates in every other empty cell. In the three-candidate cell, find the digit with three places in each of its houses. If crossing it out leaves a BUG, solving without that candidate would let you swap the choices to make another solution. A one-solution puzzle has to use the extra digit.
Check the counts across the grid before placing it. A cell with three candidates can also occur without a BUG pattern.

lessons.title: Skyscrapers clues
lessons.summary: Use the number of visible buildings from one end of a row or column.

paragraphs: Read the line from the clue end. Treat each digit as a building height. A building is visible only if it is taller than every earlier building.
Use the 9 as a cutoff. It blocks the view of every later cell. A clue of 1 puts 9 at the near end.

copy.description: Read the listed cells from left to right in the clue list. Count each height that exceeds every height seen before it.
copy.reason: Test candidate orders by counting each new tallest building. A candidate can go if no order that contains it gives the required count.

guide.start: Read the line from the clue end. Treat each digit as a building height. A building is visible only if it is taller than every earlier building.
guide.check: Use the 9 as a cutoff. It blocks the view of every later cell. A clue of 1 puts 9 at the near end.
guide.reason: Test candidate orders by counting each new tallest building. A candidate can go if no order that contains it gives the required count.

lessons.title: Sandwich sums
lessons.summary: Use the sum of the digits strictly between 1 and 9.

paragraphs: Find candidate positions for 1 and 9 in the clued line. The clue counts only the digits between those two positions.
Try a pair of endpoints and add the possible middle digits. A zero clue means the 1 and 9 touch.

copy.description: Find the possible locations of 1 and 9 in the clue’s cell list. Leave both endpoint digits out of the sum.
copy.reason: Reject endpoint pairs whose middle cells cannot reach the total. Then remove any candidate that fits no surviving assignment.

guide.start: Find candidate positions for 1 and 9 in the clued line. The clue counts only the digits between those two positions.
guide.check: Try a pair of endpoints and add the possible middle digits. A zero clue means the 1 and 9 touch.
guide.reason: Reject endpoint pairs whose middle cells cannot reach the total. Then remove any candidate that fits no surviving assignment.

lessons.title: X-sums
lessons.summary: Use the first digit from the clue end to decide how many cells to add.

paragraphs: Start at the edge cell nearest the clue. If that cell takes 3, add the first three cells, including the 3.
Try each edge candidate. Check whether a prefix of that length can reach the total without repeating a digit.

copy.description: The clue lists the line from the near edge. Read the first digit before deciding which cells add to the total.
copy.reason: If a prefix length cannot reach the total, remove the edge digit that chose it. A later candidate can go if it fits no surviving prefix assignment.

guide.start: Start at the edge cell nearest the clue. If that cell takes 3, add the first three cells, including the 3.
guide.check: Try each edge candidate. Check whether a prefix of that length can reach the total without repeating a digit.
guide.reason: If a prefix length cannot reach the total, remove the edge digit that chose it. A later candidate can go if it fits no surviving prefix assignment.

lessons.title: Following a chain
lessons.summary: Trace what is forced, then check what the endpoints prove.

paragraphs: Start with two candidates joined by a strong link. At the next candidate, look for a conflict that leads to another strong link.

blocks.title: One forced step at a time

paragraphs: Give four candidate statements the names A, B, C, and D. Suppose their links are strong, weak, strong in that order.
If A is false, D must be true. If A is true, there is no need to follow this branch. Either way, at least one endpoint is true.
A candidate that conflicts with both endpoints can be removed. The endpoints need not see each other and need not have opposite truth values.
Coloring uses two colors to record opposite states along dual links. The colors do not tell you which state is correct.
An arbitrary weak link does not force opposite colors: both of its candidates can be false. Always check which implication the next step needs.

questions.prompt: Your current statement is false. Which property can force the next statement true?
questions.explanation: A strong link rules out both statements being false.

questions.prompt: A chain proves that at least one endpoint is true. Which target can it remove?
options: A candidate conflicting with both ends
questions.explanation: That target would make both endpoints false, which the proof excludes.

questions.prompt: Two candidates have only a weak link. Must their truth values be opposite?
questions.explanation: Both can be false. A coloring step that requires opposite states needs a dual link.

lessons.title: Why two colors work
lessons.summary: Use two colors to keep track of opposite states along connected links.

paragraphs: Pick two candidates that are the only places for one digit in a house. Mark them with different colors.

blocks.title: Each pair has exactly one true candidate

paragraphs: A strong link and a weak link between the same two candidates mean that exactly one is true. This pair has a dual link.
If a candidate has another dual link, give the new endpoint the opposite color. Each step keeps the two colors opposite.
In one connected set, all blue candidates are true or all amber candidates are true. In either case, the other color is false.
If two candidates of one color conflict, that color must be false. If a target conflicts with both colors, the target must be false.
Separate sets can choose their true colors independently. Compare colors only within the same connected set.

questions.prompt: Can you color both ends of a weak link as opposites from that link alone?
questions.explanation: A weak link lets both ends be false. Opposite colors need exactly one true end.

questions.prompt: An uncolored 5 sees a blue 5 and an amber 5 in the same connected set. What can you remove?
questions.explanation: One of the colored 5s must be true. Either one rules out the uncolored 5.

questions.prompt: Two blue candidates in separate connected sets conflict. Does that prove that all blue candidates are false?
questions.explanation: Both of those sets cannot use blue together. Each set still has its own choice of color.

lessons.title: Simple Coloring
lessons.summary: Use two colors to follow the possible placements of one digit.

paragraphs: Pick one digit and find a row, column, or box with exactly two places for it. Color the candidates differently.
At each end, look for another house where that digit also has exactly two places. Keep going while you can add links, then check for a conflict within one color or a candidate that sees both.

Find two candidates for the same digit that are the only places for it in one house. Color them differently. When either candidate forms another such pair, color the new end with the opposite color. Within one connected set, placing one color rules out the other.
If an uncolored candidate sees one of each color, it can’t take the digit whichever color is placed. Erase it.

Two candidates of the same color can’t both be placed if they see each other. Erase that color throughout the connected set and place the other color. Give disconnected sets their own colors until you can link them.
Check whether every candidate for the digit in a house would disappear if you placed one color. That would leave the house without the digit. Erase that color and place the other one.

lessons.title: X-Chain
lessons.summary: Follow strong and weak links for one digit to find a candidate that sees both ends.

paragraphs: Pick a digit with exactly two places in a house. From one end, find another candidate for that digit that it sees.
Keep the new candidate if it has a house with a second two-place link. After a strong link, look for an outside candidate that sees both ends.

When a house has just two places for a digit, the pair forms a strong link. If one end is ruled out, the other must be placed. Any two candidates for the same digit that see each other form a weak link. If one end is placed, the other must be ruled out.

Use a strong link at each end of the chain and alternate the links in between. Rule out the first candidate and trace the result. At each solid link, place the next candidate. At each dashed link, rule it out. This forces the final candidate, so a cell that sees both ends loses the digit.
A Skyscraper or Two-String Kite uses three links. You can keep going through more houses as long as the links alternate and the last one is strong.

lessons.title: XY-Chain
lessons.summary: Link cells with two candidates until the same digit appears at both ends.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with two candidates. Pick one digit as the starting end. Use the other digit to find a cell you can see with exactly two candidates that includes it.
Switch to the other digit in each new cell. Continue until a far end has the starting digit and another candidate for that digit sees both ends.

Pick one candidate to cross out in a cell with two marks. That forces its other digit. Find another two-candidate cell that sees the first and shares the forced digit. Cross out that digit there and use the other mark to continue.

Stop when the last cell has to take the digit you first crossed out. One of the two ends has to take it. Erase that digit wherever a cell sees both ends. An XY-Wing uses the same argument with three cells.

lessons.title: 3D Medusa
lessons.summary: Use cells with two candidates to carry two-color reasoning from one digit to another.

paragraphs: Start at a cell with exactly two candidates and give them opposite colors. Pick either digit and look for a house where it has exactly one other spot.
Give that other spot the opposite color. If it is in a cell with two candidates, switch digits there and look for another link. Follow each connected branch.
If a link stops, check the other branches. Look for a conflict within one color or a candidate that either color would rule out.

Color the two places for a digit as in Simple Coloring. When you reach a cell with exactly two candidates, its other mark gets the opposite color. Keep following pairs in houses and in cells. In the connected set, all the candidates of one color can be placed together when that color is true.

blocks.title: When one color breaks a rule

items: One cell would get two digits of the same color.
One house would get two copies of the same digit.
Placing the color would erase every candidate from an empty cell.
Placing the color would leave a house with no place for a missing digit.

paragraphs: Any one of these checks rules out the entire color. Place the candidates of the other color in this set.

blocks.title: When either color rules out the same candidate

items: A cell contains both colors. Both choices for the cell rule out its uncolored candidates.
An uncolored candidate sees its own digit in both colors. It loses whichever color is placed.
An uncolored candidate has one color in its cell and sees its own digit in the other color. Either placement rules it out.

lessons.title: Almost locked set basics
lessons.summary: Recognize a group that is one digit away from a locked subset.

paragraphs: While looking for a naked subset, count the distinct candidate digits in a few cells that all share one house.
An almost locked set, or ALS, has N cells and N+1 distinct candidate digits. The cells must all share a house.
Two cells with {1, 4} and {4, 8} form an ALS. Their combined digits are {1, 4, 8}. A bivalue cell is the smallest ALS.

blocks.caption: Remove a digit from the whole set

paragraphs: Each case leaves two distinct digits for two cells. Those remaining digits become locked in the set.
The set cannot lose two distinct digits entirely: that would leave too few digits to fill its cells.

blocks.title: An ALS alone does not remove anything

paragraphs: The word “almost” matters. Finding an ALS does not prove which digit is absent. Another relationship must force a useful result.
This counting idea appears in WXYZ-Wing. Later ALS techniques connect several sets. Learn the count before their connection rules.

questions.prompt: Two cells in one row contain {1, 4} and {4, 8}. Is this an ALS?
questions.explanation: Two cells have three distinct candidate digits.

questions.prompt: You find an ALS. Can you immediately remove one of its digits from nearby cells?
questions.explanation: An ALS alone does not establish which digits must appear. It needs another constraint.

questions.prompt: An ALS has three cells. How many distinct candidate digits does it contain?
questions.explanation: An ALS contains one more distinct candidate digit than cells.

lessons.title: WXYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: Four cells with four digits can force a digit across houses.

paragraphs: Start with a cell that has a short candidate list. Add nearby cells that reuse those digits until four cells contain exactly four distinct digits between them.
For each digit, check whether all its copies in the four cells see one another. Keep the pattern if at least three digits pass this check.

Pick four cells with exactly four different candidates between them. Look at one digit at a time. If all the cells that could take it in the wing see one another, that digit is restricted. Only one of those cells can take it.
An almost locked set (ALS) has one more candidate digit than cells. All its cells share one house.
A common WXYZ-Wing connects two ALSs with four cells in total. This arrangement is a small ALS-XZ pattern.
The whole wing can span several houses. It is not necessarily one ALS.
If three digits are restricted, they can fill at most three cells. The fourth digit has to fill at least one. Erase it from a cell that sees every place it could go in the wing.
R4C3, R4C4, and R4C6 form a three-cell ALS with digits 1, 2, 5, and 9. R6C1 forms another ALS with candidates 1 and 9.
The two 1 candidates share box 4, so the sets cannot both use 1. At least one set must use 9.
R4C2 sees all the 9 candidates in both sets. It therefore loses candidate 9.
The restricted-digit count also explains this removal. It does not require every four-cell arrangement to have the same ALS layout.

All four cells need digits, so when every digit is restricted, each goes in exactly one cell. For each digit, erase it from cells that see all its places in the wing. With two unrestricted digits, this count gives no specific digit to erase.

references.label: Almost Locked Sets (ALS): the shared idea

lessons.title: Unique Loop
lessons.summary: Extend the two-digit uniqueness argument from a rectangle to a longer ring.

paragraphs: In a puzzle with one solution, follow two shared digits along a ring of cells. Each affected row, column, and box must meet the ring in a pair.
Follow the alternating placements around the ring. Check that you can swap the two digits and still satisfy the same houses.

copy.description: In this example, one loop cell supplies the extra choice. Remove the two shared digits from that cell.
copy.reason: If every loop cell used just the two shared digits, a swap would give another solution. An extra candidate must break the swap.
